food.text: Danish cuisine grew out of the local produce of the peasant population. It was enhanced by cooking techniques developed in the late 19th century and by the wider availability of goods during and after the Industrial Revolution.
Industrialization brought Danes more fresh meat and vegetables. Even so, rye bread and potatoes continued to be staples of the Danish diet.

Ground meats made from pork, veal or beef became widespread in Denmark during the industrial revolution. Dishes from this shift that are still popular include frikadeller (meat balls), karbonader (breaded pork patties) and medisterpølse (fried sausage).
Dairy cooperatives arrived in Denmark in the second half of the 19th century. With them, milk gained favor, although dairy products of all kinds had been consumed in smaller quantities for millennia.
In eastern parts of Sápmi, reindeer herding became a way of life in the 19th century. Before that, people there had been hunters and fishers. Today reindeer is essential to Sámi cuisine.

The introduction of wood-burning stoves and meat grinders in Denmark contributed to a range of new dishes. Among them were meat loafs, roast pork, poached cod, and stegt rødspætte, which is breaded plaice.
Desserts of stewed fruits or berries, such as rødgrød, date from the same period of new Danish cooking. So do a large variety of cakes and cookies.

Lutefisk and egg coffee were common in 19th-century Scandinavia. They have since substantially decreased in popularity or disappeared there, yet they remain common in Minnesota, where Scandinavian immigrant food traditions stayed largely unchanged.

Frk. Jensen's 1901 cook book contained traditional recipes that still form the basis of Danish Christmas cooking. The dinner is served on the evening of 24 December, with a main dish of pork, goose or duck followed by the Risalamande dessert.

art.text: Danish art was once mostly imported from Germany and the Netherlands, or made by Danes who studied abroad. From the late 18th century the situation changed radically. Beginning with the Danish Golden Age, a distinct tradition of Danish art began and has continued to flourish.
In 1871, Holger Drachmann and Karl Madsen visited Skagen in the far north of Jutland. There they quickly built up one of Scandinavia's most successful artists' colonies.

Sod roofs were the most common roof on rural log houses in Norway and much of Scandinavia until the late 19th century. Tile roofs and corrugated iron then threatened them. Just before they disappeared, national romanticism revived vernacular styles, including sod roofs, creating demand for mountain lodges and holiday homes.

Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg studied in Paris with Jacques-Louis David and was further influenced towards Neo-Classicism by Thorwaldsen. He taught at the Academy from 1818 to 1853 and was director from 1827 to 1828. He taught most of the leading artists of the period, and landscape painting came to the fore in the next generation.

The Skagen colony was soon joined by P.S. Krøyer, Carl Locher, Laurits Tuxen, the Norwegian Christian Skredsvig, and Michael and Anna Ancher. All participated in painting the natural surroundings and local people.

Helsinki's University of Art and Design was established in 1871. Finland's Design Museum, then called the Museum of Art and Design, has a collection founded in 1873. Both institutions reflect an early Finnish investment in design.

Constantin Hansen, a student of Eckersberg, was deeply interested in literature and mythology. Inspired by Niels Laurits Høyen, he developed national historical painting based on Norse mythology. He also painted many portraits, including the historical work The Constitutional Assembly.
The Swedish Society of Crafts and Design, known in Swedish as Svensk Form, was founded in 1845. It is one of the organisations that promote design in Sweden.
tags: Swedish Society of Crafts and Design

art.text: In 1914, the Danish Selskabet for Dekorativ Kunst, the Company for Decorative Arts, launched a magazine whose title means "Graceful Work". The title became the name of a new Danish style of arts and crafts, in objects and architecture, meant to rival Art Nouveau and Jugendstil.
The symbolist Jens Ferdinand Willumsen also visited the Skagen artists' community. He lived from 1863 to 1958.

Runes were still used for decorative purposes in rural Sweden, in Dalarna and on runic calendars, up until the early 20th century. In the 19th century runes were also used on Sweden's northern coast, in Medelpad, Hassela and Haverö, but they were very different from those used in Dalarna.

war.text: The English Wars were a series of conflicts that pitted the United Kingdom and Sweden against Denmark–Norway as part of the Napoleonic Wars. They are named after England, the common name in Scandinavia for the United Kingdom. Britain declared war over the neutrality of Danish trade and to stop the Danish fleet falling into French hands.

Denmark-Norway tried to stay neutral during the Napoleonic Wars, but Britain demanded that it turn over its navy. Britain attacked the Danish fleet at the Battle of Copenhagen in 1801 and bombarded the city in 1807. Most of the Danish fleet was captured after the second battle.

The First war of Schleswig ran from 1848 to 1850, and Sweden and Norway contributed considerable military force to it. By the Second war of Schleswig in 1864, the Riksdag of the Estates denounced the King's promises of military support for Denmark. Both wars shaped the Scandinavist political movement.

On 16 August 1807 Britain landed a major force in Zealand at Vedbæk without any formal declaration of war. King Christian VII and the crown prince were in Holstein with most of the Danish army, so the newly appointed commander Ernst Peymann had to face the British landing force with an inferior number of untrained militia. The British quickly began the siege of Copenhagen, and after the city fell Peymann was sentenced to death, though he was later pardoned.

After the bombardment of Copenhagen, Denmark-Norway allied with France and went to war with Britain, whose navy blockaded the two kingdoms. The remnants of the Danish fleet fought battles such as Zealand Point, Lyngør and Anholt. The Danes tried unsuccessfully to break the blockade in what became known as the Gunboat War.

On 29 August 1807, a large force of the Danish Militia was defeated at Køge by British forces under the command of Sir Arthur Wellesley. Earlier, the British had quickly begun the siege of Copenhagen, and minor skirmishes had occurred south of the capital. From 2 to 6 September the British then bombarded the city itself, using Congreve rockets, instead of storming it. On 6 September Ernst Peymann surrendered Copenhagen unconditionally.

In December 1807 the British Navy seized the Danish West Indies and occupied them for nearly eight years. The settlements of Danish India were also occupied by Britain, from 1808 to 1815. After the attack on Copenhagen the British had already captured all the Danish ships they could take back to England, burnt the rest, and taken everything of value from the naval base at Holmen. Denmark–Norway's overseas holdings thus became a casualty of its war with Britain.

Sweden, allied with Britain at the time, seized the opportunity to invade Norway in 1807. The invasion was beaten back. Britain's blockade had by then cut the lines of communication between Denmark and Norway.

Paying for the war strained Denmark. From 1807 to 1813 the war brought high inflation, with wages rising several hundred percent and grain prices even more. The government printed more and more banknotes, and from 1806 to 1813 the currency's total face value increased sixfold while the notes' real value significantly decreased. The state itself went bankrupt, and a regulation of 5 January 1813 changed the monetary system, making minor savers, people with money tied up in government bonds, and people holding higher-value banknotes relatively poor.

Baron Karl Otto Mörner, an obscure member of the Diet, was the one who first offered the Swedish crown to the young soldier Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte. Denmark was also forced to cede Heligoland to Britain after the Gunboat War.

literature.text: The Modern Breakthrough was a movement of naturalism and debating literature that replaced romanticism in Scandinavia near the end of the 19th century. The term is used about the period 1870–1890, when Scandinavian literature had a breakthrough from the rest of Europe.
Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen was largely responsible for the popularity of modern realistic drama in Europe. His plays include The Wild Duck and A Doll's House.

The Kalevala, the most famous collection of Finnish folk poetry, is referred to as the Finnish national epic. It is mainly credited to Elias Lönnrot, although he worked more as an editor and compiler. First published in 1835, it quickly became a symbol of Finnish nationalism.

The 19th century saw more systematic collection of Sámi oral poetry, influenced by broader European interest in folk culture. This work built on much earlier records, since only two joiks had been written down before.

Danish theorist Georg Brandes is often considered the wire-puller behind the Modern Breakthrough. His lectures at Copenhagen University starting 1871 and his work Main Currents in 19th Century Literature mark the beginning of the period.

The first novel published in Finnish was Seven Brothers, which appeared in 1870. Its author, Aleksis Kivi (1834–1872), died two years later, yet the book is still generally considered one of the greatest of all works of Finnish literature.

Muitalus sámiid birra (An Account of the Sámi), published in 1910 by the Norwegian Sámi author Johan Turi, is a foundational work of early Sámi prose. It gives a detailed ethnographic description of nomadic reindeer herding life and was written in Northern Sámi.

The Danish Viking revival was largely initiated by poet and playwright Adam Oehlenschläger. His 1802 poem Guldhornene (The Golden Horns) broke with earlier Classicist traditions by celebrating the nation's ancient, mythological past.

The first Sámi novel, Beaivi-Álgu ("Dawn"), was published in 1912 by Anders Larsen. Two years later, in 1914, Pedar Jalvi followed it with Muohtačalmmit ("Snowflakes"), a collection of poetry and short stories.

In 1869 Georg Brandes translated John Stuart Mill's controversial essay The Subjection of Women into Danish. He then lectured at Copenhagen University and in most of Europe, criticising romanticism. His Main Currents in 19th Century Literature, published in several volumes from 1872, became an important theoretical basis for the literature of the time.
The first Sámi novel, Beaivi-Álgu (Dawn), was published in 1912 by Anders Larsen. It was followed in 1914 by Muohtačalmmit (Snowflakes), a poetry and short story collection by Pedar Jalvi.

Danish antiquarian Carl Christian Rafn advocated the theory that the Vikings had explored North America centuries before Christopher Columbus. He published much of his work in 1837 in the Antiquitates Americanæ, considered the first scholarly exposition of the Old Norse exploration period.

Alliteration has remained a vital feature of Icelandic poetry, unlike in most other Germanic languages. From 19th-century poets like Jonas Halgrimsson onward, it has stayed a prominent feature of modern Icelandic literature.

science.text: Between 1816 and 1855, the scientist Friedrich Georg Wilhelm von Struve built a chain of survey triangulations from Hammerfest in Norway to the Black Sea. It stretched over 2,820 kilometres and gave the first accurate measurement of a meridian arc. In 2005 it was inscribed on the World Heritage List.

Hans Christian Ørsted, a Danish physicist and chemist, discovered that electric currents create magnetic fields. This phenomenon is known as Oersted's law. He was a leader of the Danish Golden Age and a close friend of Hans Christian Andersen.

Niels Henrik Abel, a Norwegian mathematician, gave the first complete proof that the general quintic equation cannot be solved in radicals. The problem had been unresolved for over 250 years. He made his discoveries while living in poverty. He had contracted tuberculosis in Paris, and it killed him on 6 April 1829 at the age of 26.

Niels Ryberg Finsen received the 1903 Nobel Prize in Medicine and Physiology for treating diseases, especially lupus vulgaris, with concentrated light radiation. He was the first Scandinavian to win the prize and is the only Faroese Nobel laureate in physiology to date. He himself suffered from Niemann–Pick disease, which inspired him to sunbathe and investigate the effects of light on living things. His health began to fail in the mid-1880s, with heart trouble, ascites and general weakness that left him working from a wheelchair, and he died in Copenhagen on 24 September 1904, with echinococcosis found at autopsy as a contributing factor.

Alfred Nobel patented dynamite in 1867, an explosive made using nitroglycerin, which was unpredictable and could explode when subjected to variable heat or pressure. On 3 September 1864 a shed used for preparing nitroglycerin exploded at the factory in Heleneborg, Stockholm, killing five people, including Nobel's younger brother Emil. Nobel later invented gelignite in 1875 and ballistite in 1887, and held 355 patents; by his death his business had established more than 90 explosives and armament factories.

Struve's chain of triangulations began at Tartu Observatory in Estonia, where he conducted much of his research. The measurements comprise 258 main triangles and 265 geodetic vertices. At publication in 1858, the flattening of the earth was estimated at one part in 294.26.

In 1824, Ørsted became the first person to produce aluminium in its metallic state, though not very pure. He reacted aluminium chloride with potassium amalgam and boiled away the mercury. The discovery went mostly unnoticed, and in 1827 he let his friend Friedrich Wöhler take over the research.

Anders Jonas Ångström, a Swedish physicist, combined the spectroscope with photography to study the Sun. In 1862 this helped prove that the Sun's atmosphere contains hydrogen, among other elements. In 1868 he published a great map of the normal solar spectrum with measurements of more than 1000 spectral lines.

Svante Arrhenius was the first to use physical chemistry to estimate how much atmospheric carbon dioxide raises the Earth's surface temperature. In 1903 he became the first Swede to win the Nobel Prize in Chemistry. His work helped in the emergence of modern climate science.

In 1824, Struve obtained a refracting telescope with a 23 cm aperture, made by Joseph von Fraunhofer, at Dorpat. With it he discovered a very large number of double stars. In 1827 he published his double star catalogue, Catalogus novus stellarum duplicium.

When Abel entered the university in 1821, he was already the most knowledgeable mathematician in Norway. He thought he had solved the quintic equation, but while trying to give a numerical example for Carl Ferdinand Degen in Copenhagen, he found a mistake in his paper. This led in 1823 to the discovery that a formula solution to a fifth- or higher-degree equation was not necessarily possible.

Arrhenius's carbon dioxide absorption values were criticised in 1900 by Knut Ångström, who published the first modern infrared absorption spectrum of CO2. Ångström's experiments seemed to show that absorption by the atmosphere was already saturated. Arrhenius replied strongly in 1901, dismissing the critique altogether.

politics.text: Russia invaded Finland in 1808 and forced Sweden to cede that province at the peace of Fredrikshamn in 1809. The inept government of King Gustav IV Adolf led to his deposition and banishment. A new constitution was introduced and his uncle Charles XIII was enthroned.

The Treaty of Kiel of 14 January 1814 dissolved the Dano-Norwegian union and ceded Norway to the King of Sweden. Widespread Norwegian resistance to union with Sweden led crown prince Christian Frederick to call a constituent assembly at Eidsvoll in April 1814. It drew up a liberal constitution and elected him to the throne of Norway.

Sweden and Denmark formed the Scandinavian Monetary Union on 5 May 1873, fixing their currencies against the gold standard at par to each other. Norway joined in 1875. It was one of the few tangible results of the Scandinavian political movement.

After the bombardment of Copenhagen, Denmark-Norway allied with France and went to war with Britain. The British navy blockaded the kingdoms and cut communication between Denmark and Norway. The conflict became known as the Gunboat War, and Denmark was later forced to cede Heligoland to Britain.

Because Charles XIII was childless, Sweden first chose Prince Christian August of Augustenborg as his successor. When Christian August died suddenly in 1810, the Swedes again picked an enemy officer: Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte, a Marshal of France and one of Napoleon's eighteen Marshals.

After a Swedish invasion in the summer of 1814, the Convention of Moss of 14 August specified that Christian Frederik must resign. Norway would keep its independence and its constitution within a personal union with Sweden. He abdicated on 10 August and returned to Denmark.
The offer of the Swedish crown to Bernadotte was first extended by Baron Karl Otto Mörner, an obscure member of the Diet. Bernadotte was a young soldier and a Marshal of France at the time.

The Norwegian parliament, the Storting, elected King Charles XIII of Sweden as king of Norway on 4 November 1814. Norway kept its constitution in this union with Sweden. It only attained full independence in 1905.

The Second war of Schleswig in 1864 was a brief but disastrous war between Denmark and Prussia, supported by Austria. Prussia conquered Schleswig-Holstein. After Prussia's success in the Franco-Prussian War, a Prussian-led German Empire was created and a new balance of power was established in the Baltic region.

When Prince Christian August of Augustenborg, the commander in chief of the Norwegian army, died suddenly in 1810, the Swedes again chose an enemy officer as successor to Charles XIII. They picked Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte, a Marshal of France who had originally been one of Napoleon's eighteen Marshals.

The Finnish-Norwegian border on the Scandinavian Peninsula was established after extensive negotiation in 1809. The common Norwegian-Russian districts were not partitioned until 1826. Finland had been an autonomous grand duchy within the Russian Empire since 1809.

philosophy.text: Søren Kierkegaard, born in 1813, is widely considered the first existentialist philosopher. He stressed how one lives as a "single individual", highlighting authenticity, personal choice and commitment, and the duty to love. He prioritized concrete human reality over abstract thinking.

Philosophy was the first academic subject in Finland. In the 19th century Finnish philosophy was dominated by Hegelianism, and J. V. Snellman, who represented Hegel's thinking and was influenced by German idealism, has been regarded as Finland's national philosopher.
The 19th century saw the arrival of various evangelical free churches in Sweden. Towards the end of the century secularism also emerged, leading many to distance themselves from church rituals.

Søren Kierkegaard's theology was a major influence on twentieth century theology. He aimed his writings at Christendom, and especially the Danish State Church, which he thought made people lazy in their religion. Many citizens were officially Christians without knowing what it meant, and he tried to awaken them to the need for unconditional religious commitment.

Kierkegaard was extremely critical of Christianity as a state-controlled religion, such as the Church of Denmark. His theological work focused on Socratic Christian ethics and the individual's subjective relationship to the God-Man Jesus Christ, which came through faith.

The first academic to draw attention to Kierkegaard was fellow Dane Georg Brandes. Brandes gave the first formal lectures on Kierkegaard in Copenhagen and helped bring him to the attention of the European intellectual community.
After J. V. Snellman, the professor of philosophy was Thiodolf Rein, who founded the Finnish Philosophical Association in 1873. He was succeeded in 1905 by Arvi Grotenfelt, a Neo-Kantian.

In Sweden it remained illegal until 1860 for Lutheran Swedes to convert to another confession or religion. The Dissenter Act of 1860 allowed people to leave the Church of Sweden, but only by joining another denomination.

Georg Brandes published the first book on Kierkegaard's philosophy and life, Søren Kierkegaard, ein literarisches Charakterbild, in 1879. Adolf Hult said it was a "misconstruction" of Kierkegaard's work and "falls far short of the truth".

The first German translation of Kierkegaard's work appeared in 1861. Albert Bärthold began the first substantial program of translating him into German in 1873, and Christoph Schrempf translated his main works from 1909 onwards.

The most prominent Finnish philosopher at the turn of the century was the moralist and social anthropologist Edvard Westermarck. He became professor of applied philosophy in 1906 and was also a professor at the London School of Economics from 1907 to 1930.

Academic research into Old Norse religion began in the early 19th century, influenced by romanticism. Many scholars framed their approach through nationalism, directly equated religion with the nation, and projected modern national borders onto the Viking Age past.
Hermann Gottsche published Kierkegaard's Journals in 1905. It had taken academics 50 years to arrange them.

culture.text: In the 19th century, Europeans rediscovered the Viking past in a movement called the Viking revival, which often added heroic overtones typical of the Romantic era. The word Viking is not a medieval term and entered Modern English only during the 18th century. Etymologists frequently trace it to writers describing those who set out to raid and pillage, and it derives from the Old Norse víkingr, meaning a sea-rover or pirate. The Romantics falsely lumped Viking exploits together and romanticized them as heroic adventure.

Norse mythology was little known outside Scandinavia until the 19th-century Viking revival. With the widespread publication of Norse myths and legends, references to the Norse gods and heroes spread into European literary culture, especially in Scandinavia, Germany, and Britain.
Norway saw a rise in nationalism in the 19th century. Having spent 400 years in a union with Denmark and then a union with Sweden, Norwegians began looking back to their Viking Age kings and sagas.
The 19th century saw evangelical free churches arrive in Sweden. Towards the end of the century secularism also grew, leading many people to distance themselves from church rituals.

In 1867 the Tune ship, the first Viking ship ever unearthed, was excavated in Østfold, Norway. It gave new knowledge about the Vikings and their culture, and other excavations raised Norwegian awareness of the Viking past.

The Victorian adventure writer H. Rider Haggard wrote an epic adventure in the style of the Nordic sagas, Eric Brighteyes, in 1890. Antiquaries such as George Webbe Dasent likewise brought Scandinavian mythology back to the notice of many people in Germany and England.
In 1880 Norway uncovered the Gokstad Ship, a fine example of Viking Age craftsmanship. Central to its construction is the clinker-built method, a hallmark of Scandinavian boat-building tradition.

The word Norseman first appears in English in the early 19th century. The earliest attestation given in the Oxford English Dictionary is from Walter Scott's 1817 Harold the Dauntless, and the word has no particular basis in medieval usage.
